prize_parts.citation: For the development of halide perovskites as high-efficiency solar cell absorbers

statement.case_for: Halide perovskites are a structurally simple ABX3 family whose defect tolerance, strong absorption and long carrier diffusion lengths took solution-processed photovoltaics from a few percent to well over 25 percent certified efficiency in about a decade. The principle is clear and quantitatively demonstrated, the result has been reproduced worldwide, and it opens a genuinely new capability (cheap thin-film and tandem photovoltaics, and optoelectronics generally) that can be explained to a broad audience. The proposed three-person attribution follows the chain of discovery: Miyasaka made the first perovskite-sensitized cell, and Park and Snaith are the groups that turned it into the solid-state, high-efficiency device.
statement.case_against: Credit is genuinely contested among Miyasaka, Park, Snaith, Gratzel, Kanatzidis and Seok, and any three-person cut will be criticised. Operational stability and lead content are unresolved, so a citation framed around practical impact could be seen as premature. In the opening ballots perovskites drew support from only four of eight members, whereas targeted protein degradation (B054) was in five top-three lists, so my first-place view is not obviously the committee's centre of gravity.

responses.point: Zou ranks perovskites first and agrees on the Miyasaka-Snaith-Park trio, but warns that stability and lead toxicity could argue for waiting for deployment evidence.
responses.response: I share the concern but would separate it from the discovery itself. The prize recognises that a defect-tolerant semiconductor can be a high-efficiency absorber, which is settled by independent reproduction, not whether modules last twenty-five years. I would draft the citation around the absorber material and efficiency, not around commercial deployment, so that the open stability question does not weaken it. I would still like Zou's view on whether Kanatzidis or Gratzel should displace Park.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks Car-Parrinello first because attribution is a clean two-person credit and the method is overdue after forty years of validation.
responses.response: I agree that B059 has the cleanest attribution on our list, and I rank it among my top eight. My reservation is the overlap with the 1998 DFT prize, and with metadynamics and machine-learned potentials that also involve Parrinello, so the discovery would have to be defined narrowly as unifying electronic structure and dynamics. I would not call it more urgent than perovskites, but I accept it as a strong alternative and would like Aqvist to say what the committee would cite beyond a method already overlapping a recognised field.

responses.point: Aili ranks ionizable lipid nanoparticles first, arguing the 2023 Medicine prize recognised nucleoside modification and left delivery chemistry unrecognised, so timing is favourable.
responses.response: The chemical principle, pKa-tuned lipids that are neutral in circulation and charged in the endosome, is clear and the impact is unequivocal. I qualify the claim of favourable timing, because the 2023 prize makes the vaccine story hard to separate from Karikó and Weissman, and Aili himself notes that any three names leave out MacLachlan, Hope or Madden. Until we can identify which lipid-design step was decisive and who owns it, I would not put B036 ahead of a candidate whose credit chain is more traceable.

responses.point: Sparr ranks biomolecular phase separation first as a new concept of cellular organisation grounded in multivalency and interfacial physics, supported by fifteen years of confirmation.
responses.response: As a physicist I find the polymer-physics framing attractive and would credit Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen as the core. My serious reservation is that the concept is still under debate regarding which cellular structures are truly phase separated in vivo and what function this has, and Sparr concedes the same issue. I think a prize now would risk crediting a framework before the field has separated physiological condensates from in vitro droplets, and the split between experiment and Pappu and Mittag's theory is unresolved.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks long-range electron transfer through proteins first, calling Gray and Winkler the decisive pair and the recognition overdue.
responses.response: The attribution is clean and the framework is textbook, which counts strongly. My question is what exactly the new capability is: Marcus theory was already recognised in 1992, and I would want the committee to be clear whether the citation recognises a discovery in protein tunnelling or an extension of recognised theory. If Brzezinski can show that the experimental proof on modified proteins was decisive and separable from the theory, I would take B043 more seriously as a configuration.

uncertainties: Whether Park or Gratzel/Kanatzidis/Seok has the stronger claim to the third place beside Miyasaka and Snaith
Whether stability and lead toxicity make a perovskite citation premature for part of the committee
Whether the committee prefers targeted protein degradation (B054), which had the broadest top-three support, and how to choose three of its eight names
Exact dates and relative contributions of the 2009-2012 perovskite papers are from memory and not verified in the materials I may read
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile: none of the shortlisted candidates is linked to Lund University or to my own nanowire, thermoelectric or molecular-motor work. I note only that fellow Lund members Somfai and Sparr are colleagues, which is not a recusal issue.
